source.text:
If you have a full-time job and roughly five hours a week to spare, the platform you choose for learning Python matters more than almost any other decision you will make. Pick a program sized for people with twice your free time and you will likely stall somewhere around month three, which is exactly where most learners give up: only around 12 percent of people finish MOOCs. I spent the past few months working through syllabi, trial accounts and learner forums for the main contenders, and the best answer for working professionals is not the one most roundup lists give.

Start with what actually gets you hired. Hiring managers consistently say they care more about what you can build than about the credentials you hold, but a recognisable certificate still helps you get past HR filters and gives your study a structure. The ideal platform for a busy professional therefore combines three things: Python taught through real datasets, a certificate employers recognise, and a total time commitment you can realistically finish.

Coursera is where most people start, and for good reason. Its Professional Certificates from Google, IBM and Meta carry instantly recognisable names. They are not interchangeable, though. The Google Data Analytics certificate, nine courses estimated at six months at 10 hours a week, is built around R, Google Sheets, SQL and Tableau rather than Python. It is an excellent foundation in business analytics, but if Python is your goal it is simply the wrong program.

The IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate is the one usually recommended to Python learners. Across 11 courses it covers Excel, SQL, Python, Jupyter notebooks and IBM's own Cognos Analytics. The problem is scale. Coursera's own estimate for the IBM program is roughly eight months at 10 hours a week, which stretches to well over a year and a half at five hours a week. A good share of that time also goes to Excel and Cognos, a proprietary dashboard tool that rarely appears in analyst job postings, where Tableau dominates. Many learners who finish end up paying for a separate Tableau course afterwards.

The Meta Data Analyst certificate is leaner at five courses, or about five months at 10 hours a week, and it does use Python, pandas and Matplotlib, with a heavy tilt toward statistics and marketing analytics. If you work in marketing it is worth a look; for general analysis work it is narrower than it first appears.

Cost is the other catch. Coursera Plus, the all-access subscription that unlocks all three certificates, now runs $79 a month or $599 a year, and a monthly plan keeps billing for every month you fall behind schedule. For someone studying five hours a week, that adds up quickly.

edX takes a more academic approach. There is no subscription plan; you pay per course or program, with verified certificates and MicroMasters credentials from institutions such as MIT and Harvard. The standout is Harvard's CS50P, Introduction to Programming with Python, which offers a free certificate through cs50.harvard.edu, or $219 for an edX verified certificate. It is superb, but it is a general programming course of roughly 100 to 150 hours, not a data analysis program, so you will still need to learn pandas and visualisation somewhere else.

That brings us to DataCamp, which I think is the best fit for most working professionals. Its lessons are short, run in the browser and have you writing Python against real datasets from the first session, which suits 30- to 45-minute study blocks on weeknights. Its career tracks cover pandas, data cleaning, visualisation and SQL, with guided projects you can put straight into a portfolio. Crucially, DataCamp's certifications are now accredited and recognised for academic credit, so you no longer have to trade hands-on learning for a credential that carries weight with employers.

A couple of other options deserve a mention. Dataquest's Beginner Python for Data Analysis path, at $33 to $49 a month, is similarly project-driven, and the Python Institute's PCEP exam, at $69 for a single attempt, gives you a formal entry-level Python credential if you want one on top.

The bottom line: if you need Python specifically, skip Google's R-based certificate. If you can reliably find ten or more hours a week, IBM's program is solid. But for a working professional with five hours a week who wants hands-on projects and a credible certificate, DataCamp is the most efficient route, with CS50P as a free supplement for programming fundamentals.
